generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, synthesis is what a literature review is built on. You do not report each source in turn; you make them speak to each other, noting where they agree and where they conflict, and you build from them a position of your own. Agreement across several sources strengthens a claim, while a sharp disagreement complicates it. Drawing these together into your own argument is synthesis.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students bringing the same three sources to an essay.

{{learner-a}} writes a paragraph on each source in turn: the first found this, the second argued that, the third reported something else. Each summary is accurate, and the three never meet. No claim of {{learner-a}}'s own emerges, and the reader is left with three reports side by side. This is summary, not synthesis.

{{learner-b}} makes the three sources speak to each other. Two agree on a point, while the third, better supported, does not; {{learner-b}} sets the agreement against that dissent and argues, from the tension, that the point holds but is narrower than first claimed. The sources become evidence for {{learner-b}}'s own position. This is synthesis.

Both students used the same three sources. Only {{learner-b}} drew them together into an argument of their own, which is what makes writing synthesis rather than summary.
generatedProse.summary: Synthesis means drawing several sources together into an argument of your own, making them speak to each other rather than summarising each in turn. You can now tell synthesis apart from summary and identify a synthesis move across sources. With analysis, evaluation and synthesis in hand, you can put the critical skills to work on purpose.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s writing synthesis rather than summary?

items.text: {{learner-b}} set the sources against each other and built a claim of their own that none stated alone.
{{learner-b}} wrote a separate, accurate paragraph on each source.

feedback.correct: That's right. Making the sources speak to each other to build a claim of your own is synthesis.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} did across the sources, rather than reporting each one.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} synthesised: setting the sources against each other and building a claim none stated alone. Separate paragraphs, more sources or fuller quotes are still summary.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
